items.name: AOD-9604
items.benefits: Preclinical findings: AOD-9604 reduced body-weight gain and increased fat oxidation and lipolysis markers in obese mice given experimental infusions. In a separate rabbit osteoarthritis model, joint injections reduced cartilage-degeneration scores and lameness, with better results when combined with hyaluronic acid. These results do not establish human fat-loss or cartilage-repair benefits. FDA's clinical evidence review found inadequate evidence to support obesity treatment by any route; human weight-loss studies largely failed to show benefit versus placebo.

FDA concluded available evidence did not support obesity efficacy for any route; most reviewed studies failed to show benefit versus placebo. Human subcutaneous and topical exposure evidence was not identified in the assessment. Category rationale: Weight & Metabolism follows its original anti-obesity development and mouse fat-metabolism findings; the separate joint-repair signal remains preclinical. This classification does not imply human efficacy.

Original 2001 article read in the author-uploaded full text at ResearchGate after publisher/PubMed fetch errors. Obese mice received 14-day infusion by implanted mini-osmotic pumps; reduced weight gain, increased fat oxidation, and circulating glycerol were measured. DOI 10.1038/sj.ijo.0801740. Category rationale: Weight & Metabolism follows its original anti-obesity development and mouse fat-metabolism findings; the separate joint-repair signal remains preclinical. This classification does not imply human efficacy.

Original abstract read through the indexed PubMed source; 32 rabbits with experimentally induced osteoarthritis, joint injections, lower cartilage-degeneration scores and shorter lameness than saline; combination performed better. Not human or subcutaneous cartilage-repair evidence. Category rationale: Weight & Metabolism follows its original anti-obesity development and mouse fat-metabolism findings; the separate joint-repair signal remains preclinical. This classification does not imply human efficacy.
